lesson.title: Darwin's Evidence: Finches, Pigeons, and a Theory Takes Shape
lesson.summary: During and after his voyage on HMS Beagle, Darwin gathered a body of evidence, from finch beaks in the Galapagos to pigeon breeding at home, that together pointed toward natural selection as a real mechanism for evolutionary change.
lesson.body:
Building on the idea, already circulating before him, that species were not fixed and that the Earth was old enough for gradual change, Charles Darwin still needed to explain how such change could actually happen. Much of his evidence for that came from a five year voyage, from 1831 to 1836, as the naturalist aboard the survey ship HMS Beagle, during which he observed plants, animals, fossils, and geology across South America and the Pacific.

Among the specimens Darwin collected in the Galapagos Islands were a group of small birds, later recognized, with the help of the ornithologist John Gould who examined them after the voyage, as a set of closely related finch species. Their beaks differed noticeably from island to island, thick and strong on islands where hard, tough seeds were the main food source, slender and pointed on islands where insects or softer food predominated. This pattern, of a single ancestral group diverging into forms suited to different local conditions, became one of the clearest illustrations that a population could change and diversify over time in response to its environment.

Darwin carried Lyell's Principles of Geology with him during the voyage and was deeply influenced by it. Seeing firsthand geological evidence of slow, ongoing processes reshaping the landscape convinced him that biological change, too, could accumulate gradually if given enough time, exactly the kind of deep time Lyell's uniformitarianism provided.

After returning to England, Darwin spent years studying domesticated plants and animals, and took up pigeon breeding himself. He observed that breeders, by simply choosing which individual pigeons to mate based on desired traits, could produce dramatically different varieties, from fantails to pouters, all within a human lifetime and all descended from a single wild ancestor. Darwin used this artificial selection as an accessible analogy, if breeders could reshape a species that much on purpose in a matter of decades, some comparable selective process operating in nature, over vastly longer stretches of time, could plausibly produce the diversity of life he saw around the world.

The final piece came in 1838, when Darwin read Thomas Malthus's essay on population, first published in 1798, which argued that populations tend to grow faster than their food supply can support, leading to an ongoing struggle for existence among individuals competing for limited resources. That was the missing mechanism. If more individuals are born in each generation than the environment can support, then individuals with even a slight heritable advantage in that struggle would tend to survive and reproduce more successfully than others.

Darwin held onto these ideas for two decades, continuing to gather supporting evidence, before publishing. In 1858, the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace, working independently in the Malay Archipelago, sent Darwin a manuscript outlining a strikingly similar theory of natural selection, arrived at through his own observations of variation and the struggle for existence. Their ideas were presented jointly to the Linnean Society of London in 1858, and Darwin published his fuller argument, On the Origin of Species, the following year, in 1859. Both Darwin and Wallace deserve credit for independently arriving at natural selection as the mechanism behind evolutionary change.
